# Dynamic Electricity Pricing: a Real Experiment

<p style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace; font-size:.8rem; letter-spacing:.02em;">
Difference in differences · Placebo tests · Event study · Causal forest · LightGBM · Integer programming · Python and R · 9 tests
</p>
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The business question

A utility or a grid operator that sends a high price for a few hours wants to know four things.
How much does consumption fall, and does it come back later? Who responds? How do I measure the
response without a control group? And on which days and hours should I send the signal so that
the peak of a local network actually falls? Pricing teams in any business with peak capacity,
from transport to telecoms, ask the same questions. Few data sets let them be answered with a
real price change. This one does.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The data

In 2013, the Low Carbon London project put about 1,100 London households on a dynamic tariff. At
08:00 the day before, each one received on the in-home display, and by text message if they
wanted, the price of each part of the next day: **High (67.20 p/kWh), Normal (11.76) or Low
(3.99)**. Everyone else in the trial, about 4,500 households, paid a flat 14.228 p/kWh. Smart meters
recorded every household every half hour from late 2011 to February 2014: **167.9 million
readings of 5,566 households**. There were **69 High events** (26 of 3 hours, 34 of 6 hours, most
of them at 17:00) and **92 Low events**, on 115 days.

Two facts about the design matter for what follows. The dynamic group was **recruited from the
trial's smart meter customers, not drawn by lot**: the project balanced the two groups on
demographics, but volunteers can differ from the rest. And a bill safety net promised that no
participant would pay more than on the old tariff. The identification below therefore rests on
comparing the same households before, during and after 2013, against the flat-rate group, with
placebo tests; and the bills computed here are before that safety net.

Most meters were installed during the first half of 2012, so the analysis uses households with at
least 80% of their readings in each of three windows: July to December 2012, all of 2013, and
January and February 2014. That leaves **878 dynamic-tariff households and 3,345 flat-rate ones**;
880 of the flat-rate households, drawn to match the distribution of consumption before the trial,
form the comparison group. Quality rules removed 115,453 duplicate readings, 719,230 readings from
days on which a meter reported only zeros, 5,560 empty or off-the-clock readings and 13 implausible
values. Every event starts on the hour and lasts whole hours, so the analysis uses hourly sums
without losing any price change: 25.5 million household-hours.
:::

::: {.rh-section}

## Method

**How much consumption moves.** Hourly consumption is regressed on indicators for "dynamic-tariff
household in a High hour" and "in a Low hour", with fixed effects for each household at each hour
of the day in each period and for each date at each hour of the day. The second set absorbs the
weather, holidays and anything else that hits both groups at the same time; the first absorbs each
household's routine. Errors are clustered by household (R, `fixest`). The same regression is run in
levels and in logs.

**Placebos.** The 2013 calendar is copied onto the same weeks of 2012 (364 days earlier, same
weekday) and of 2014 (364 days later), when everyone paid the flat rate. If the comparison were
picking up something other than the price, these fake events would show an effect too. The second
half of 2013 against its 2012 copy gives a triple difference.

**Shift and rebound.** An event study measures the response in each hour from 4 hours before to 3
hours after each 3-hour and 6-hour High block and each standalone Low block, by quarter, with the
response by month and by start hour. These profiles are estimated on the difference between the
two groups' mean consumption hour by hour, with the same fixed effects, and a household bootstrap
(300 draws) for the intervals; on the headline coefficients the two routes agree.

**Who responds.** For each household, the change in consumption in High hours relative to its own
routine, in 2013 minus the same quantity on the 2012 placebo hours, goes into a causal forest (R,
`grf`) with features measured before the trial: daily use, the share used between 16:00 and 20:00,
variability, the winter-to-summer ratio and the base load. Because the dynamic group volunteered,
the forest also models the chance of being in it. A calibration test checks whether the forest can
rank households, and the ranking is compared with simply sorting by consumption.

**Measuring without a control group.** Settlement of demand response usually compares the event
with a baseline: the mean of the same hour on the 10 previous event-free days, sometimes scaled to
the hours just before the event. These are set against LightGBM models trained only on flat-rate
households, with the household's own history, temperature and calendar, with and without the
flat-rate group's consumption in the same hour, and scored on Normal hours of event-free days.

**Designing the calendar.** A feeder of 200 flat-rate homes from the panel, winter of 2013. With
the event-study response (including the shift before and after), scaled by quarter and by how many
homes are on the tariff, an integer program (PuLP) chooses days and start hours to minimise the sum
of the monthly peaks, given at most K events a month. It is compared with the trial's own calendar
and with sending the signal only to the fifth of homes that use most. Only the observed prices are
used.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Results

**A High hour cuts use by 5%; a Low hour raises it by 3%.** In a High-price hour, dynamic-tariff
households used **28.4 watts less** than their own routine and the flat-rate group imply (95%
interval 23 to 34 W), **5.0%** in logs, on an average of about 0.44 kWh in those hours. In a Low
hour they used **16.3 W more** (10 to 23 W), **+3.3%**. Against a price 5.7 times the Normal one,
that is an elasticity of about **-0.03**; the Low price, a third of Normal, gives the same -0.03.
Households do respond, but little.

**The placebos are zero.** The same calendar laid on the flat-rate weeks of 2012 gives -2.3 W for
High hours (-10.9 to +6.3) and -7.1 W for Low hours (-14.7 to +0.4); on January and February 2014,
after the tariff ended, +2.0 W and +2.0 W. The time of day and the season of the events do not
fake a response, and no habit outlived the tariff. Comparing the second half of 2013 with its 2012
copy gives -19.8 W for High (-32 to -8) and +21.0 W for Low (+10 to +31).

**Mostly cut, little shifted, and a winter thing.** In 3-hour High blocks the cut is 15, 34 and 31 W
in the three hours, followed by a small rebound of 7 to 8 W in the next two. The 6-hour blocks,
mostly 17:00 to 23:00 and preceded by a Low block, show about 11 W more in the hours before, 21 to 43
W less during, and no rebound after. Standalone Low blocks raise use by 35 to 55 W while they last.
The High response is **-56 W in January and February** and -49 W in November, and close to zero from
June to September; the Low response is the reverse, largest in summer. That is not fatigue, since
the response comes back in autumn: on winter evenings there is lighting, heating and cooking to
cut. The 6-hour block at 17:00 gets -40 W, twice the -20 W of 6-hour blocks at other times.

**Bigger users cut more, and the forest does not rank better than that.** The causal forest's mean
effect for the dynamic group is -25.9 W (±6.8), in line with the regression. Its calibration test
does not show that it can tell households apart (coefficient on the predicted difference 0.43,
±0.74), and the fifth it ranks as most responsive cut 24.6 W, the same as everyone. Sorting by
consumption before the trial does better: the lowest fifth (3.3 kWh a day) cut 9 W, the highest
(18.8 kWh a day) 47 W. **86% of the dynamic households paid less** than on the flat rate, before the
safety net: £12.73 a year on average (median £9.34) on a mean bill of £477, mostly because the
Normal price was below the flat one. Among the fifth that used the largest share between 16:00 and
20:00, 67% paid less; among the fifth with the smallest share, 95%.

**A forecast baseline does not replace the control group.** At the level of one household and one
hour every baseline errs by about 44% of consumption, and LightGBM is no better than "10 of 10"
(mean error 0.167 against 0.169 kWh). In High hours, "10 of 10" measures -24.5 W, close to the
-28.4 W of the regression. LightGBM measures -31.9 W, but finds -7.4 W on flat-rate households that
faced no price at all. The same-day adjusted baseline measures **-14.7 W, half the response**,
because the hours used for the adjustment carry the Low price and the shift before the event: on
flat-rate households it adds 13.5 W. In Low hours every baseline overstates the response (+26.7 to
+33.9 W against +16.3). The model helps to forecast; the comparison group and the placebos are what
identify the effect.

**When matters more than how often.** On a feeder of 200 homes with a winter peak of 215 kW, with
everyone on the tariff, one optimised 6-hour High event a month cuts the mean monthly peak by 4.8 kW
and four a month by **10.1 kW (4.7%)**; beyond six a month there is nothing left to cut. The trial's
own winter calendar, with 16 six-hour events, cuts 1.8 kW, and its 3-hour events none, because they
did not fall on the days and hours of the feeder's peaks. Sending the signal only to the fifth of
homes that use most keeps 4.0 kW, 40% of the cut with 20% of the homes notified. With four 6-hour
events a month, 622 kWh are cut in High hours and 111 kWh added outside them: most of the energy is
not used, rather than moved.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Limits

The dynamic group volunteered, and the bill safety net meant that no one could lose money; a tariff
imposed on everyone, without that guarantee, could see a different response. The placebos rule out
a seasonal or time-of-day artefact, not every difference between volunteers and the rest. Only
three price levels were tried, so the elasticity holds for these jumps and the simulator does not
extrapolate to other prices. The feeder is built from household meters, not measured at a
substation. The demographic group of each household (Acorn), which the project used, is not in the
public file, so heterogeneity is described by consumption before the trial instead. The data are
from 2013: appliances, heat pumps, electric cars and batteries have changed how much load can move.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Applied to your business

This is the
<a href="../oquant.html#packages">Custom Forecasting package</a> applied to dynamic pricing. For a
utility, a retailer of energy or any business that prices peak capacity, the same pieces run on
your own meters or transactions: a price test read with a control group and placebos, the response
by hour and by customer, a baseline checked against the experiment, and a calendar of price events
chosen for the peaks that cost you.
:::
